The addition of solute (salt) to a small volume of water will increase the concentration of the solution, and therefore increase the osmolality.  Osmoreceptors in the medulla will detect this increase in osmolality and stimulate the neurohypophysis to increase ADH secretion.  The increased ADH will cause the insertion of aquaporins into the apical membrane of the cells of the collecting duct, increasing the permeability of the kidney to water.  This will lead to an increase in the amount of water reabsorbed into the blood, increasing the blood volume.  The increased blood volume will increase the pressure entering the glomerulus, increasing the glomerular filtration pressure.  This will increase the GFR.

Labyrinthitis is the correct answer. This is inflammation of the entire labyrinth, including the half-circular canals, the vestibular apparatus and the scala media. It often follows an infection, such as a URI, and can cause vertigo, nausea, vomiting, tinnitus and hearing loss.  BPPV is caused by free rattling of otoconia in the semicircular canals, and so the vertigo is triggered by changes in head position. It does not cause other symptoms such as tinnitus or hearing loss.  Meniere's disease is more chronic and is characterised by recurrent episodes of vertigo. These episodes last for a few days and includes the triad of fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and a feeling of pressure in the ear.  Vestibular neuronitis is a viral neuritis of the vestibular nerve. It presents with sudden onset vertigo, nausea and vomiting, but without the other labyrinth symptoms such as tinnitus and hearing loss.  Vestibular paroxysmia is a less common condition characterised by brief episodes of vertigo (the unsteadiness feeling) which are triggered by specific facial positions or movements. The attacks last usually less than a minute and are not associated with the other symptoms of the disorders of the inner ear.

Cushing’s disease is a form of hypercortisolemia caused by a pituitary-secreted ACTH. It is characterised by high cortisol levels. Taking glucocorticoids such as prednisolone to treat asthma would suppress negative feedback of cortisol on the pituitary gland, leading to even higher ACTH levels and making the patient’s symptoms worse. Patients with Cushing’s disease and other forms of hypercortisolemia should not be given glucocorticoids.Glucocorticoid receptor antagonists such as ramipril are not crossed on the HPA axis and therefore will not affect cortisol levels. Patients with primary hyposecretion of cortisol (e.g. Addison’s disease) may be given these to make them glucocorticoid resistant. In patients with Cushing’s disease, somatic cells are not responding to the high levels of cortisol. This is because the pituitary is producing too much ACTH, causing the adrenals to produce too much cortisol. If the pituitary were not causing the adrenal to produce excess cortisol, then you would not have hypercortisolemia. Radiation therapy to treat a pituitary adenoma will remove the pituitary cells that are producing the excess ACTH, and therefore will be a treatment option for Cushing’s disease.

Sentinel cells are a type of phagocyte that reside in peripheral tissues, and act as the first line of defence against infection. They can recognise the presence of microbes and then migrate to the nearest lymph node, where they present the microbial antigens to the T helper cells. This allows the activation of adaptive immunity.  Natural killer cells are lymphocytes, and are a type of cytotoxic cell. Clopidogrel is an anti-platelet drug that prevents initiated platelets from activating other platelets and starting a chain reaction. It is metabolised into a compound which is a competitive inhibitor of the cycle-oxygenase domain of the P2Y12d receptor on the surface of platelets. This prevents aggregation of platelets. Aspirin is also an anti-platelet drug but it works in a different way. It causes irreversible acetylation of a serine residue in the cycle-oxygenase domain of the COX enzymes. This means that the enzyme is inactive and so cannot produce thromboxane A2, which is necessary for proliferation of platelets and so aspirin prevents platelet proliferation.

HCN4 channels are hyperpolarised cyclic gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels. Stimulation of beta 1 adrenoreceptors (predominantly found in cardiac tissue) via the sympathetic nervous system results in an increase in adenylyl cyclase activity and thus in cAMP. cAMP activates protein kinase A which in turn opens L-type calcium channels. This results in an influx of calcium into the cell. This calcium then is able to bind to ryanodine receptors on the SR, triggering further calcium release from the SR. The increased intracellular calcium will result in increased inotropy (i.e. increased force of contraction). It will also have a lusitropic effect (i.e. speed up relaxation of the myocytes). Chronotropy refers to the effect on heart rate.

Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy is the most common form of diabetic neuropathy. It is characterised by sensory loss in a stocking pattern – so, you start to lose sensation from your feet and the lower legs and it then ‘symmetrical’ which means that it affects both feet equally.  Acute painful diabetic neuropathy, which is less common, tends to affect specific nerves and is more likely to affect the upper portions of the legs. The pain is usually crampy and can be very disabling.  Autonomic diabetic neuropathy can cause a wide variety of symptoms including:  – GI: diarrhoea and gastroparesis (stomach doesn’t empty properly so you feel full quickly and take longer to digest food)  – GU: erectile dysfunction in men and urinary incontinence or hesitancy in women  – CV: postural hypotension (when you stand up quickly you feel lightheaded and dizzy because blood pools in your legs)  – respiratory: sleep apnoea  – thermal – reduced sweating so you lose the ability to control your body temperature  – other: sexual


Other complications of diabetes vision: diabetic retinopathy – blood vessels in the retina leak and cause swelling and fluid to build up under the retina, flattening of the macula and so loss of visual acuity. In advanced cases the retina can detach or bleed to the point of blindness.  Microalbuminuria and macroalbuminuria are signs of kidney disease.

Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT I) is an enzyme found on the outer mitochondrial membrane. It catalyses the reversible reaction between Acyl-CoA and carnitine to form Acylcarnitine. Acylcarnitine can then be transported across the mitochondrial membrane via the carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. Carnitine acyltransferase II (CAT II) is found on the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyses the reverse reaction, converting acylcarnitine back into Acyl-CoA and carnitine. The Acyl-CoA is now in the matrix and can be used in beta-oxidation. ATP is used in the first step and is regenerated in the last step.

Spinal stenosis is the most likely diagnosis based on the history. The classic history of spinal stenosis is pain in the legs on walking which is worse with standing/walking upright and relieved with sitting/crouching. This is because the narrowing of the spinal canal compresses the nerves only when the spine is upright due to calcification of facet joints which push the nerves. The fact that the SLR is classically negative also suggests spinal stenosis as opposed to a prolapsed disc. There would be no focal neurology. There is often some x-ray/MRI abnormalities such as canal narrowing, central retrolisthesis, irregular contours of the canal due to ligament hypertrophy and sometimes a 떠ed marrow signal in the pars intervertebralis.  The other options are unlikely as:Peripheral arterial disease: pain is colicky and bilateral and often in the feet, calves or thighs. It is also usually relieved by using a pedal pumpDesmid: central/paracentral scar tenderness and dermatomal tenderness for nerve root compressionChronic mechanical back pain: pain is usually worse with movement and better with restMetastatic spinal cord compression
